root_cause.text: In RDS connection info gathering functions (rds_for_each_conn_info, rds_walk_conn_path_info), the per-item stack buffer is not zeroed before being partially filled by visitors, causing uninitialized stack memory (including alignment holes and uninitialized fields) to be copied to userspace via rds_info_copy().
root_cause.evidence: The commit message states: "rds_for_each_conn_info() and rds_walk_conn_path_info() both hand a caller-allocated on-stack u64 buffer to a per-connection visitor and then copy the full item_len bytes back to user space via rds_info_copy() regardless of how much of the buffer the visitor actually wrote." It further describes that "rds_ib_conn_info_visitor() and rds6_ib_conn_info_visitor() only write a subset of their output struct when the underlying rds_connection is not in state RDS_CONN_UP," leaving fields like max_send_wr, rdma_mr_max, etc. uninitialized, and the reproduction shows leaked kernel pointers. The fix adds `memset(buffer, 0, item_len)` before the visitor call.

candidates.rationale: Part of the for loop that iterates over hash heads; each iteration invokes the visitor on an unzeroed stack buffer, leading to potential information leak.
Hash traversal macro that sets up the connection pointer for each iteration; each iteration results in a call to the vulnerable visitor without zeroing the buffer.
Direct call to the visitor function with a stack-allocated buffer that is not zeroed. If the visitor only partially fills the buffer, uninitialized data can be leaked to userspace via rds_info_copy.
Control flow statement that skips to the next iteration after the visitor call; part of the vulnerable code path but does not directly cause the information leak.
Assigns the connection path pointer used as an argument to the subsequent vulnerable visitor call on an unzeroed buffer.
Second visitor call on a connection path object with an unzeroed stack buffer; similar to the first call, partial writes can leak uninitialized stack memory.
Control flow statement associated with the second visitor call; part of the vulnerable loop structure.

vuln_statements.explanation: This visitor call passes the unzeroed stack buffer to a function that may only partially fill it. Any uninitialized stack memory, including alignment holes or unset fields, can then be copied to userspace via rds_info_copy(), directly causing the information leak.

Second visitor call with the same unzeroed stack buffer. The buffer is not zeroed before this call, so uninitialized stack data remains and can be leaked to userspace if the visitor does not overwrite all bytes.

This macro iterates over connections in the hash list. Each iteration calls the visitor with the same stack buffer (allocated once for the function). Without zeroing the buffer per iteration or before the loop, data from previous iterations or uninitialized memory can persist and be leaked.
Assigns the connection path pointer used as argument to the subsequent visitor call. This statement is part of the vulnerable code path where the unzeroed stack buffer is passed to the visitor.

Part of the outer for loop that iterates over hash heads. Each iteration of this loop (and the nested hlist traversal) will invoke the visitor on the same unzeroed stack buffer, contributing to the potential leak of uninitialized stack memory.

Controls flow to skip to the next iteration when the visitor fails. Although the continue statement itself does not cause the leak, it is part of the control structure that repeatedly calls the visitor without zeroing the buffer, thus enabling the vulnerability.

Same as above but belongs to the second visitor call (in the rds_walk_conn_path_info function). It also appears after the visitor check and, together with the loop structure, allows repeated use of the unzeroed buffer, which can leak uninitialized data.
